content:
The [Distance Between Two Points Calculator](/distance-between-two-points-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Straight-line distance between two points in 2D. Enter your point 1 — x, point 1 — y, point 2 — x and point 2 — y and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Find the straight-line (Euclidean) distance between two points on a coordinate grid. It is the same maths as Pythagoras' theorem: the distance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the differences in x and in y. Surveyors, map-makers, game developers and anyone working with coordinates use it constantly — from measuring a plot of land to checking how far apart two objects are on a screen. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Distance Between Two Points Calculator

Start by entering your point 1 — x, then entering your point 1 — y, entering your point 2 — x and finally entering your point 2 — y. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the x and y coordinates of both points.
2. Read the straight-line distance — the midpoint is shown too.
3. Negative coordinates work the same way.

## Formula

d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). For (1, 2) and (4, 6): d = √((4 − 1)² + (6 − 2)²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Distance Between Two Points Calculator](/distance-between-two-points-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. The distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6) is 5: the x difference is 3, the y difference is 4, and √(3² + 4²) = 5. The midpoint is (2.5, 4). Try the same figures in the [Distance Between Two Points Calculator](/distance-between-two-points-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Point 1 — x: 1, Point 1 — y: 2, Point 2 — x: 4, Point 2 — y: 6), the [Distance Between Two Points Calculator](/distance-between-two-points-calculator) returns Distance: 5, Change in x: 3, Change in y: 4, Midpoint: (2.5, 4). The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## It is Pythagoras in disguise

Draw a horizontal line from the first point and a vertical line from the second and they meet at a right angle, forming a right triangle. The distance between the points is the hypotenuse, the x difference and y difference are the legs, and c = √(a² + b²) gives the answer. That is why the distance formula and the hypotenuse formula are the same calculation.

## Distance vs. how far you travel

This is the straight-line distance — as the crow flies. The distance you actually travel along roads, or in a grid of city blocks, is longer: city-block (Manhattan) distance is |x₂ − x₁| + |y₂ − y₁|, which for (1, 2) to (4, 6) is 3 + 4 = 7 rather than 5. Use the straight-line distance for maps and geometry, and the road distance for journeys.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- The order of the points does not matter — the distance is the same either way.
- The midpoint is the point exactly halfway between the two.
- This is straight-line distance; road distance is longer.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the distance formula?

d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Subtract the coordinates, square both differences, add them, and take the square root. You can see it in action in the [Distance Between Two Points Calculator](/distance-between-two-points-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.

### How far apart are (1, 2) and (4, 6)?

5 units. The x difference is 3 and the y difference is 4, so the distance is √(9 + 16) = 5. Try it with your own numbers in the [Distance Between Two Points Calculator](/distance-between-two-points-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does the order of the points matter?

No. Swapping the two points gives the same distance, because the differences are squared. Try it with your own numbers in the [Distance Between Two Points Calculator](/distance-between-two-points-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the midpoint?

The point halfway between the two: ((x₁ + x₂) ÷ 2, (y₁ + y₂) ÷ 2). For (1, 2) and (4, 6) it is (2.5, 4). Try it with your own numbers in the [Distance Between Two Points Calculator](/distance-between-two-points-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
